subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Find the radical centre of the circles x² + y² − 4x − 6y + 5 = 0, x² + y² − 2x − 4y − 1 = 0, x² + y² − 6x − 2y = 0.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Sr. Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.54 — SAQ chapter 7 System of Circles (chapter runs pp.54-56), answer 53.1, on a ★★★ Super Scoring Page (SSP 54). insider_note: Examiners give one mark per usable line, so write both radical axes as separate numbered equations before solving them together — a single jumbled block loses marks even when the final coordinate is correct.

steps.label: Find the first radical axis
steps.margin_note: First mark. Any two of the three circles give a valid radical axis — this solution takes S and S′ first.
lines: Radical axis of S, S′ is S − S′ = 0
steps.why: The radical axis of two circles is the line S − S′ = 0 — subtracting cancels the x² and y² terms because both circles are written with coefficient 1 on x² and y², leaving a straight line.
common_mistakes: Subtracting the circles in the wrong order and carrying a sign error into the rest of the answer.
Not writing S, S′, S″ first — three circles are easy to mix up without labels.
steps.memory_tip: Radical axis = one circle minus another, same letter order every time, so the sign never flips halfway through.

steps.label: Find the second radical axis
steps.margin_note: Second mark. This uses the SAME S from step 1, paired now with the third circle.
lines: Radical axis of S, S″ is S − S″ = 0
steps.why: A third circle gives a second, independent radical axis; two lines are enough to fix the one point where all three axes meet.
common_mistakes: Taking S′ − S″ instead of S − S″ — still valid, but then it must be solved consistently with equation (1), not mixed with it.
Losing the constant term while simplifying.
steps.memory_tip: Keep S as the fixed reference circle in both subtractions — one fixed point of comparison, two moving partners.

steps.label: Solve the two axes
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Any correct elimination method earns this mark, not only the scaling shown here.
steps.why: Two linear equations in x and y have exactly one common solution, and that common point is the radical centre — the point with equal power with respect to all three circles.
common_mistakes: Substituting the y value into the wrong equation.
Arithmetic slip turning 18/6 − 11/6 into something other than 7/6.
steps.memory_tip: Scale one equation so the x-coefficients match, then subtract to remove x first — the same elimination used for any pair of straight lines.

steps.label: State the radical centre
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark, for the final coordinate pair.
steps.why: This point has equal power with respect to all three circles — it is the unique meeting point of the three pairwise radical axes.
common_mistakes: Writing the coordinates as (11/6, 7/6) — swapping x and y.
Leaving the answer as a rounded decimal instead of the exact fraction.
steps.memory_tip: The radical centre is a POINT, not a line — box a coordinate pair here, not an equation.

steps.label: The diagram
steps.margin_note: The question does not ask for a diagram, so this earns no marks. The three circles are schematic, not drawn to the true scale of these equations.
steps.why: Any two of the three circles' radical axes meet at the same point — the figure shows this concurrency, which is the geometric fact the algebra proves.
common_mistakes: Thinking a diagram is required to solve this algebra — it is not; the figure only shows why the two lines above meet at one point.
Drawing the third radical axis through a different point — all three are concurrent by the same theorem.
steps.memory_tip: Three circles, three radical axes, one meeting point — that point is called the radical centre because it belongs to every pair at once.
